demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette:
Leilani Fono is a 61-year-old Samoan-American woman who has worked as a security guard at a large regional shopping mall for the past eleven years. She is single, lives alone in a small apartment, and describes herself as someone who has always taken her responsibilities seriously - someone who believed, before that evening, that careful attention could prevent most harm.

Fourteen months ago, during a late-night shift, Leilani was responding to a reported disturbance near the mall's east loading dock. Moving quickly through a poorly lit corridor, she pushed open a heavy fire door without knowing that a young maintenance worker was standing directly on the other side. The door struck him with considerable force, and he fell, sustaining a fractured skull and a serious traumatic brain injury. Leilani was the first to reach him, kneeling on the concrete floor and pressing her hands to his head while calling for help, watching blood spread beneath her palms. The sounds of his laboured breathing and the particular quality of the light in that corridor - the sickly yellow of the emergency strip lighting - were the last things she registered with full clarity before something in her memory seems to have simply stopped recording.

She knows she stayed until the paramedics arrived. She knows she gave a statement. But those minutes are gone, and no amount of effort has recovered them. The gaps in her memory have become a source of profound distress in themselves. Leilani cannot accept that she does not know exactly what she did or failed to do in those missing moments, and the incompleteness of what she can recall drives her into long cycles of review - going over and over the sequence of events, turning each detail she does retain in her hands like a fragment of broken glass, searching for the shape of the whole. She has spent entire nights at her kitchen table doing this, reconstructing timelines in a notebook, convinced that if she can just find the right angle of approach, the memory will finally cohere and she will understand what she is responsible for.

Yet the more she dwells, the stranger the memory becomes. When she does manage to call up the scene - the corridor, the door, the sound - it arrives with a disturbing flatness, as though she is reading a report about a woman she has never met. She can narrate what happened without feeling that it happened to her, and this emotional distance, rather than offering relief, frightens her. She has come to believe that her numbness is itself evidence of something broken in her character, that a person who truly felt remorse would not experience her own memory as belonging to a stranger. This interpretation feeds her compulsion to keep analysing, to keep searching the record of events for a version she can actually inhabit and grieve.

Her rumination is relentless and takes several forms simultaneously. She dwells on what she did wrong - the speed of her approach, her failure to check the door, her inadequate knowledge of who was working in that corridor that night. She searches for reasons the event happened at all, cycling between punishment narratives and random-universe narratives with equal exhaustion. And she overanalyses the details with a persistence that has colonised her waking hours. This sustained cognitive effort does not produce resolution; instead, it keeps the event perpetually present and perpetually unprocessed, so that the memory remains fragmented and alien, which in turn compels further analysis. At work - the very environment where the accident occurred - she finds herself pausing at every fire door, rehearsing the moment, checking and rechecking, her mind still trying to close a loop that will not close.

Over the past year she has become increasingly isolated. Colleagues have noticed her distraction. Her supervisors have raised concerns about her concentration on shift. She has not told anyone what she is doing in her own mind during those long quiet hours on patrol.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a conversation with the maintenance worker's sister, who contacted her to say that he had survived but would never fully recover. Leilani had hoped, she realised, that certainty about his outcome would end the rumination. It did not. What she is most afraid of is that nothing ever will.
